questions.q: What is the value of $\sqrt[3]{26}$ corrected up to three decimal places?

\begin{aligned}
x+\Delta x & =26 \\
27+\Delta x & =26 \quad[\because \text { let } x=27]
\end{aligned}

\Delta x=-1

We have, $\quad y=x^{1 / 3}$
Differentiate w.r.to ' $x$ '

\begin{aligned}

d y & =\frac{1}{3} x^{-\frac{2}{3}} d x \\
d y & =\frac{1}{3 \cdot x^{2 / 3}} d x=\frac{1}{3 .(27)^{\frac{2}{3}}}(-1) \\
\Delta y & =\frac{-1}{3(9)}=-\frac{1}{27} \approx-0.037 \\
3 \sqrt{26} & =y+\Delta y=3+(-0.037)=2.962
\end{aligned}

Hence, option (3) is correct.

m: n=-1: 4

questions.q: The period of revolution of planet $A$ around the sun is 8 times that of $B$. The distance of $A$ from sun is how many times greater than that of $B$ from the sun?
questions.solution:
If $T_A$ and $T_B$ are the time periods of planet $A$ and $B$ around the sun respectively, then

T_A=8 T_B

According to Kepler's law,

\begin{array}{rlrl} 
& & T^2 & \propto R^3 \\
\Rightarrow & \left(\frac{T_A}{T_B}\right)^2 & =\left(\frac{R_A}{R_B}\right)^3 \\
\Rightarrow & & \frac{R_A}{R_B} & =\left(\frac{T_A}{T_B}\right)^{2 / 3}=\left(\frac{8 T_B}{T_B}\right)^{2 / 3} \\
& & =(8)^{2 / 3}=\left(2^3\right)^{2 / 3}=2^2 \\
\Rightarrow & & \frac{R_A}{R_B} & =4 \Rightarrow R_A=4 R_B
\end{array}

questions.q: Young's modulus for perfectly rigid body is
questions.solution: In perfectly rigid body, there is no change in its dimensions on applying a deforming force, therefore strain in the perfectly rigid body is zero. $\therefore$ Young's modulus $=\frac{\text { Stress }}{\text { Strain }}=\frac{\text { Stress }}{0}=\infty$ Therefore, Young's modulus of a perfectly rigid body is infinite.

questions.q: According to the Hooke's law the force required to change the length of a wire by $l$ is proportional to
questions.solution:
Given, change in length, $\Delta l=lL=$ original length (say)
According to Hooke's law,

\begin{aligned}
& \text { Stress } \propto \text { Strain } \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\text { Stress }}{\text { Strain }}=\text { constant } \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{\text { Stress }}{\text { Strain }}=\text { Young's modulus } \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{F / A}{\frac{\Delta l}{L}}=Y \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{F L}{A \Delta l}=Y \\
& F=\frac{Y \cdot A \Delta l}{L} \\
&
\end{aligned}

Since, $Y, A, L$ are constant.
Hence, $\quad F \propto \Delta l$
But $\quad \Delta l=l\therefore \quad F \propto l$

questions.q: The efficiency of an ideal Carnot engine working between temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$ is $1 / 3$. If the temperature of the sink is reduced by $40 \%$, then its efficiency will be
questions.solution:
Efficiency of Carnot engine, $\eta=\frac{1}{3}$
But $\eta=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}$
where, $T_1=$ and temperature of fource
$T_2=$ temperature of sink.

\therefore \quad \frac{1}{3}=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1} \Rightarrow \frac{T_2}{T_1}=1-\frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow \frac{T_2}{T_1}=\frac{2}{3}

When temperature of sink is reduced by $40 \%$, then its new temperature, $T_2^{\prime}=T_2-40 \%$ of $T_2$
=T_2-0.4 T_2

\Rightarrow 
T_2^{\prime}=0.6 T_2

Now, efficiency of Carnot's engine

\begin{aligned}
\eta^{\prime} & =\left(1-\frac{T_2^{\prime}}{T_1}\right) \times 100=\left(1-0.6 \frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) \times 100 \\
& =\left(1-0.6 \times \frac{2}{3}\right) \times 100=0.6 \times 100=60 \%
\end{aligned}

questions.q: When the area of cross-section of a stretched wire is halved and tension is doubled, the speed of propagation of transverse waves along it becomes $k$ times the initial speed. Then, $k$
questions.solution:
Speed of transverse wave in stretched wire is given as

v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{m}}

where, $T=$ tension in the wire
and $\quad m=$ mass per unit length of wire.

\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{M / l}} \quad\left[\because m=\frac{M}{l}\right] \\
& =\sqrt{\frac{T l}{M}}=\sqrt{\frac{T l}{V \cdot \rho}} \\
& {[\because M=V \cdot \rho]} \\
& =\sqrt{\frac{T l}{A \cdot l \cdot \rho}} \\
& {[\because V=A \cdot l]} \\
& v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{A \rho}} \Rightarrow v \propto \sqrt{\frac{T}{A}} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{v_2}{v_1}=\sqrt{\frac{T_2}{T_1} \times \frac{A_1}{A_2}} \\
& \text { Given, } \quad A_2=\frac{A_1}{2}, T_2=2 T_1 \\
&
\end{aligned}

$\therefore$ From Eq. (i), we get

\begin{aligned}
& \frac{v_2}{v_1}=\sqrt{\frac{2 T_1}{T_1} \times \frac{A_1}{\frac{A_1}{2}}}=\sqrt{4} \\
